reading.ours: two units of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — an instrument check, and it is printed first because nothing below it means anything until it passes. The true ratio is a little UNDER 2: both sides pay the driving loop once, so the exact expectation is (2u + L) / (u + L) with L the loop and u one unit, which at sixteen dependent steps per unit puts it around 1.9. A reading below 1.5 means this process could not resolve a deliberate doubling, and the runner voids the report rather than printing prices under it.

reading.ours: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: the same body again, over its own copy of the same state
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — the noise floor. The two sides are identical code over identical, separately-allocated state, so the true ratio is 1.00 exactly and every departure from it printed here was produced by this machine at this moment. The rule that follows is the one the whole table is read under: NO RATIO CLOSER TO 1.00 THAN THIS GAP IS A READING. It also bounds the per-row noise figure, which is the same idea measured again inside every pair — each pair times its floor twice, once before our side and once after, and prints how far the two disagreed.

reading.ours: update the entity, flush, and the subscription fires — per identity delivered
reading.floor: store the field and call the handler at once, with no flush
reading.caveat: The price of deferred delivery against none at all. The floor calls the handler inside the write, so a handler can see half of a frame's update; it is not a floor anything with once-per-flush delivery can reach, and `subscribe.deliver-vs-queue-at-flush` is the floor that is. The gap between the two pairs is what deferral itself costs by hand; the rest of this ratio is the identity registration, the stamp, the enlist and the frame.

reading.ours: update the entity, flush, and the subscription fires — per identity delivered
reading.floor: store the field, queue the entity once, and call the handler for each queued entity at flush
reading.caveat: Both sides deliver once per flush, after every write of the frame has landed, so no handler sees half an update. One write per identity per frame is the worst case for us: nothing is saved by coalescing. Ours per delivery: the update path, the stamp, enlisting the slot's effects on the frame, and the frame running each body. The floor per delivery: one store, a flag test and a push on the write, a flag clear and the call at flush. The fixed cost of a frame is divided by a thousand deliveries here; `flush.empty-vs-noop` prices it on its own. What ours adds over the floor: the handler is registered against the identity, so a writer does not need to know who is listening.

reading.ours: effectService.createEffect([column slot of 'title'], [], h) — the narrowest signal the engine has
reading.floor: store the field, queue the entity once when the moved name is 'title', and call h for each queued entity at flush
reading.caveat: The one column that moved is the one subscribed to, on both sides, and both deliver once per flush after every write of the frame has landed. A column of an entity is its own identity in ours, minted by `holdColumn`, and a write marks only the column slots that exist, so a `note` write does not reach a `title` subscriber at all. The mint is outside the clock (one per entity, at build); inside it ours pays the write path, the column mark, the enlist and the frame, against the floor's store, string compare, flag test and push on the write, and flag clear and call at flush.
